cards.front: In Java's operator summary, what does the % operator compute?
cards.extra: It is the arithmetic remainder operator, e.g. 7 % 3 is 1. For negative operands the sign of the result follows the dividend, not the divisor.

cards.front: What does the unary ! operator do?
cards.extra: It is the only unary operator that works on boolean; it cannot be applied to numbers, where you would instead use ~ for a bitwise complement.

cards.front: What does the instanceof operator compare?
cards.extra: It yields true if the object is an instance of that class, a subclass of it, or a class implementing that interface. It is classified as a relational operator for precedence.

cards.front: Which operator is an unsigned right shift?
cards.extra: It shifts bits right and fills the leftmost positions with zeros. By contrast >> is the signed right shift and fills with the sign bit (sign extension).

cards.front: How do && and & differ in result type?
cards.back: && takes two booleans; & is a bitwise AND
cards.extra: The conditional operators &&/|| are boolean-only and short-circuit. The bitwise operators &, |, ^ combine the bits of integral values.

cards.front: The ternary operator ?: is shorthand for which statement?
cards.extra: Form: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse. It uses three operands, which is why it is also called the ternary operator.

cards.front: Which unary operator requires an operand and leaves numbers positive anyway?
cards.extra: Numbers are positive without it, so it exists mostly to make a sign explicit. Unary - negates an expression instead.

cards.front: What does the ++ operator do?
cards.extra: It exists in prefix (++x) and postfix (x++) forms, which differ in the value the expression yields. Its counterpart -- decrements by 1.

cards.front: Which operators have the highest precedence in Java?
cards.extra: The precedence ladder descends: postfix, unary, multiplicative, additive, shift, relational, equality, bitwise AND/XOR/OR, logical AND/OR, ternary, then assignment last.

cards.front: Among operators of equal precedence, in which direction are binary operators evaluated?
cards.back: Left to right (assignment operators are right to left)
cards.extra: So a - b - c means (a - b) - c, while a = b = c assigns c to b first. Parentheses override both rules.

cards.front: Which precedence does the assignment operator = have relative to all other operators?
cards.extra: That is why a = b + c computes the addition before the assignment. Only the ternary ?: sits immediately above it.

cards.front: Why is x += 1 preferred to x = x + 1?
cards.back: Compound assignment applies the binary operator then assigns, in one step
cards.extra: Semantically they are equivalent for a simple variable, but x += 1 names the left operand once, which avoids evaluating a complex target expression twice.

cards.front: Where do the relational operators sit relative to equality operators in precedence?
cards.extra: So a < b == c < d compares the two boolean results. Precedence alone explains why x + 1 < y * 2 needs no parentheses.

cards.front: Which three operators are short-circuiting in Java?
cards.extra: The second operand of &&/|| and the unused branch of ?: are not evaluated when the outcome is already determined, which matters when the left side has side effects.

cards.front: Applying ~ to a byte whose bits are 00000000 produces which bit pattern?
cards.extra: The unary bitwise complement inverts every bit: each 0 becomes 1 and each 1 becomes 0. Applied to an int the pattern is 32 bits wide.

cards.front: Java uses == rather than = to test equality. What can go wrong with == on two non-null objects?
cards.extra: Two distinct String objects with identical characters are ==-unequal; use equals() for value equality. For primitive values == is correct.

cards.front: What does + do when either operand is a String?
cards.back: Concatenates, converting the other operand to a string
cards.extra: If one operand is a String the whole + is string concatenation, so "a" + 1 + 2 gives a12 while 1 + 2 + "a" gives 3a.

cards.front: How do prefix and postfix ++ differ in the value they evaluate to?
cards.back: Prefix yields the incremented value; postfix the original
cards.extra: In a statement on its own line the difference is invisible; it only matters when the increment is embedded in a larger expression such as an assignment or an argument list.

cards.front: What is a Java array?
cards.back: A container object holding a fixed number of values of a single type
cards.extra: If you need a growable sequence, use a collection such as ArrayList; an array's length cannot change after it is created.

cards.front: When is the length of an array established?
cards.back: At creation - and it is fixed afterwards
cards.extra: Declaring a variable only declares the type; the length appears when the new expression or the initializer runs.

cards.front: Where does array element indexing start?
cards.back: At 0, so the n-th element is at index n-1
cards.extra: An array of 6 elements has valid indices 0 to 5, and an array's last valid index is length - 1.

cards.front: Which syntax creates a 10-element int array?
cards.extra: The size lives in the creation expression, not in the type: the type is written int[] and stays bare. The shortcut {...} instead sizes the array to the number of values.

cards.front: In a multidimensional array such as String[][] names, what is each component?
cards.back: Another array - it is an array of array references
cards.extra: Each element must be accessed with the matching number of indices, names[i][j]. Rows may have different lengths, producing jagged arrays.

cards.front: How does a Java 2-D array differ from a C or Fortran 2-D array?
cards.back: It is not one contiguous memory block, so rows may vary in length
cards.extra: Each row is a separate array referenced from the outer array. That is what permits irregular (jagged) arrays, which a contiguous rectangular block could not represent efficiently.

cards.front: Which property gives an array's size (not a method)?
cards.extra: Unlike String, which uses the method length(). For arrays of arrays, read each row's own length rather than assuming they are equal.

cards.front: What does System.arraycopy(src, srcPos, dest, destPos, length) require of the caller?
cards.extra: The five parameters are source, its start index, destination, its start index and the number of elements to copy. No array is allocated for you.

cards.front: What does Arrays.copyOfRange(a, from, to) return?
cards.extra: Because it allocates the destination itself, it needs fewer lines than System.arraycopy. The end index is excluded, as with substring.

cards.front: Given Arrays.copyOfRange(c, 0, 9), is the element at index 9 of c copied?
cards.extra: Off-by-one here is the classic bug: the result has to - from elements, so (0, 9) copies indices 0 through 8 only.

cards.front: Which Arrays method sorts an array using multiple threads?
cards.extra: The sequential alternative is sort(). Parallel sorting is faster on multiprocessor systems for large arrays, but has overhead that hurts tiny ones.

cards.front: Which Arrays method finds the index of a value in a sorted array?
cards.extra: It relies on the array already being sorted; on an unsorted array the result is unspecified. Arrays.equals() compares two arrays, and Arrays.fill() writes one value to every index.

cards.front: What does the compiler assign to a local variable that is not initialized?
cards.extra: Fields do get a reasonable default; locals do not, and reading an unassigned local is a compile-time error. This is why a declared but unallocated array blows up.

cards.front: Which control-flow statement runs a block only if a test is true?
cards.extra: If the test is false, control jumps to the end of the statement. The if-then-else variant adds a second path for the false case.

cards.front: Are the braces of an if-then clause required?
cards.back: Optional, but only for a single statement
cards.extra: Omitting them is legal but brittle: add a second statement later and it silently falls outside the clause, and the compiler cannot catch it. Braces are the safer convention.

cards.front: In an if / else if / else if chain, how many clauses' statements run?
cards.back: Only the first whose condition is true
cards.extra: Later conditions are not even evaluated, so a value matching several tests (76 >= 70 and 76 >= 60) is graded by the earliest branch in source order.

cards.front: How does do-while differ from while?
cards.back: The condition is tested at the bottom, so the body runs at least once
cards.extra: With while a false condition on entry skips the body entirely. Use do-while when the action must happen before the check makes sense.

cards.front: Which for-loop part executes exactly once, as the loop begins?
cards.extra: The termination expression is tested before each iteration and, when false, ends the loop. The increment expression runs after every iteration, even though it may decrement.

cards.front: What is the scope of a variable declared in a for loop's initialization?
cards.back: From its declaration to the end of the loop's block
cards.extra: It is therefore usable in the termination and increment expressions but not after the loop. Declaring the counter there limits its lifetime and avoids reuse bugs.

cards.front: Which is recommended: the enhanced for or the general three-clause for?
cards.back: The enhanced for, whenever it can be used
cards.extra: It is more compact and readable when you only need each element of an array or collection in turn, without index arithmetic.

cards.front: How does an unlabeled break behave inside nested loops?
cards.extra: To leave an outer loop from inside an inner one, label the outer statement and use break label;.

cards.front: After a labeled break search;, where does control continue?
cards.back: At the statement immediately after the labeled statement
cards.extra: It does not jump to the label. The label merely names the statement to leave, so the statement flagged search: is abandoned entirely.

cards.front: What does an unlabeled continue do?
cards.back: Skips the rest of the current iteration of the innermost loop
cards.extra: Control then re-evaluates the loop's condition and proceeds with the next iteration. It does not exit the loop, unlike break.

cards.front: A loop counts letter 'p' by iterating characters; what happens if the continue is removed?
cards.back: The count becomes wrong, counting every character
cards.extra: Without the guard the counting statement runs on non-matching characters too. The original 9 'p's become 35 's example.

cards.front: What does the return statement do?
cards.back: Exits the current method, optionally returning a value
cards.extra: In a void method, use the bare return; form. In a non-void method, the type of the returned expression must match the declared return type.

cards.front: Which keyword produces the value of a switch expression from inside a case block?
cards.extra: return would be ambiguous between leaving the method and leaving the switch. yield is followed by a non-void expression that becomes the switch's value.

cards.front: What is a Java expression?
cards.back: A construct that evaluates to a single value
cards.extra: The value's type depends on the elements used: cadence = 0 yields an int because assignment returns a value of the left operand's type.

cards.text: If you do not use parentheses, the evaluation order of an expression follows operator {{c1::precedence}}.
cards.extra: Higher-precedence operators are applied before lower ones, so a + b / c divides first. Parentheses let you state the intended order explicitly instead of relying on this.

cards.front: Why should you add parentheses to a compound expression even when precedence alone is unambiguous?
cards.back: It makes the code easier to read and to maintain
cards.extra: Anyone reading (a + b) / c knows the intent at a glance; a + b / c forces the reader to recall the precedence table.

cards.front: Which three kinds of statements exist in Java?
cards.back: Expression statements, declaration statements and control-flow statements
cards.extra: Expression statements are expressions (assignment, ++/--, method call, object creation) terminated by ;; declaration statements declare variables; control-flow statements govern execution order.

cards.front: What ends an expression statement?
cards.extra: That terminator is what turns an expression into a complete unit of execution, e.g. result++; or new Object();.

cards.front: What is a block?
cards.back: A group of zero or more statements between balanced braces
cards.extra: A block may be used anywhere a single statement is allowed, which is why braces can appear in a method body, an if clause or a bare scope.

cards.front: Does 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 evaluate to true in Java?
cards.extra: Binary floating point cannot represent 0.1, 0.2 or 0.3 exactly, so the rounded sum differs. Use BigDecimal or an epsilon comparison when decimal precision matters.

cards.front: What type does the expression cadence = 0 evaluate to?
cards.back: The declared type of the left operand
cards.extra: An assignment is an expression, not just a statement, so int cadence; int x = (cadence = 0); compiles. This chaining also allows a = b = c.

cards.front: Which primitive selector types does a switch not accept?
cards.extra: The accepted primitives are byte, short, char and int. Wrapper types, enums and String are also accepted.

cards.front: Name the selector types a switch does accept.
cards.back: int, char and their wrappers, plus enums and String
cards.extra: The wrappers are Character, Byte, Short and Integer. String selectors are allowed since Java SE 7.

cards.front: What does fall through mean in a switch statement?
cards.back: Statements after the matched label run until a break, even past later labels
cards.extra: Subsequent case labels are not tested. That is why each break is needed to stop execution at the end of the intended case.

cards.front: What ends a switch statement and jumps past the switch block?
cards.extra: Without it, execution falls through into the following cases. A final break is not required but is recommended so that adding cases later stays safe.

cards.front: Which case labels handle selector values that no case matches?
cards.extra: There is at most one default, and it may appear anywhere in the block - commonly last for readability. Without it an unmatched value runs no case statements.

cards.front: Can two case labels share one statement?
cards.back: Yes - stack labels one after another, with no break between them
cards.extra: That is the legitimate use of fall through: the shared statement executes when either label matches. Commonly used to group equivalent values such as 28-day months.
cards.example:
switch (month) {
    case 2:
    case 4:
    case 6:
    case 9:
    case 11:
        days = 30;
        break;
    default:
        days = 31;
}

cards.front: When must you use if-then-else rather than switch?
cards.back: When the test is a range or boolean condition
cards.extra: A switch matches a single integer, enum or String value against constants; it cannot express score >= 80 && score < 90 or a boolean selector.

cards.front: How is a String switch selector compared to its case labels?
cards.extra: To accept case variations, lowercase the selector first with toLowerCase() and write lowercase labels.

cards.front: What happens when the selector variable of a switch statement is null?
cards.extra: A selector is an object for String, wrapper and enum types, so null is possible. Guard with a null check before switching.

cards.front: Starting with which Java SE version is the switch expression syntax available?
cards.extra: The traditional switch statement remains available and its semantics did not change; the new form is an addition, not a replacement.

cards.front: What is the new switch case label syntax in a switch expression?
cards.extra: Only the code to the right of a matched arrow label runs, so nothing falls through. That code may be an expression, a block, or a throw statement.

cards.front: Does fall through still happen with arrow (->) case labels?
cards.back: No - each label's code is the only code that runs
cards.extra: Fall through is limited to the traditional colon form. Avoiding it is one of the main motivations for the new syntax, since accidental falling is a common bug.

cards.front: How many constants can one arrow case label match?
cards.extra: e.g. case 1, 3, 5, 7 -> .... In the colon syntax the same effect needs stacked labels or a companion break structure.

cards.front: How does an arrow case produce a value when its body is a single statement?
cards.extra: No yield needed. Only when the body is a block does the value have to be produced explicitly, because a block's last statement does not automatically supply it.

cards.front: Which statement yields the value of a switch expression from a block body?
cards.extra: return was rejected because it is ambiguous between leaving the method and leaving the switch expression. yield is a branch statement, valid in any case block.

cards.front: What does a switch expression require that a switch statement does not?
cards.back: Exhaustiveness - a matching label for every possible value
cards.extra: A non-exhaustive statement silently does nothing. Non-exhaustive expressions are a compile-time error, which turns a hidden bug into a build failure.

cards.front: When can an enum switch expression omit the default clause?
cards.back: When it covers all known constants of the enum
cards.extra: The compiler still inserts a synthetic default for the case where a constant is added later; it is never reached in normal runs and throws IncompatibleClassChangeError if it is.

cards.front: What does the compiler's synthesised default clause throw in an exhaustive enum switch?
cards.extra: It fires only if a new enum constant appeared after the code was compiled, which means the switch no longer covers every value. It cannot be reached during a normal run.

cards.front: Can a switch expression use the traditional case L: colon form?
cards.back: Yes, but fall through applies and values must be produced with yield
cards.extra: This lets you migrate incrementally: the expression does not force the arrow syntax, though mixing the two styles in one block is confusing.

cards.front: What happens today when you switch on a null selector?
cards.extra: Switch does not accept null selectors; null handling was a preview feature in Java SE 17. A null-tolerant switch required an explicit null case to arrive.

cards.front: Why was the old switch block's single-scope treatment a problem for the expression form?
cards.back: A variable declared in one case might be visible in other cases
cards.extra: The whole block shared one scope, so name collisions and unclear lifetimes were possible. The arrow form gives each case body its own block scope.

cards.front: Starting with which Java SE version can you declare a local variable with var?
cards.extra: The compiler infers the real type from the initializer, so you write var message = "hi"; instead of String message = "hi";.

cards.front: Once a var variable is created, can its type change?
cards.back: No - the inferred type is fixed at declaration
cards.extra: The type is not dynamic or weakly typed. var only saves you typing it out; all the usual compile-time checks still apply to the inferred type.

cards.front: Where can var not be used?
cards.extra: It is restricted to local variables in methods, constructors and initializer blocks. Some languages reuse var for parameters; Java deliberately does not.

cards.front: What must every var declaration include, and why?
cards.back: An initializer - because null and missing values have no type
cards.extra: The compiler cannot infer a type from nothing, so var greetings; and var x = null; both fail to compile.

cards.front: In for (var item : list), what is var inferred from?
cards.back: The element type of the iterated array or collection
cards.extra: For a List<String>, item becomes String. The same works in a try-with-resources declaration.

cards.front: What is autoboxing?
cards.back: The compiler automatically converting a primitive to its wrapper object
cards.extra: For example int becomes Integer, double becomes Double. The reverse conversion, object to primitive, is called unboxing.

cards.front: What is unboxing?
cards.back: The compiler automatically converting a wrapper object to its primitive
cards.extra: Triggered when an object of a wrapper class is passed to a method expecting the primitive, or assigned to a primitive variable. The typical call inserted is intValue().

cards.front: When does the compiler apply autoboxing?
cards.back: When assigned to a wrapper variable, or passed to a wrapper parameter
cards.extra: These are the two listed cases. Nothing else triggers it - for instance, a method expecting long does not box an int into a Long.

cards.front: Why does List<Integer> ints = new ArrayList<>(); ints.add(42); compile?
cards.back: The compiler boxes 42 into an Integer automatically
cards.extra: The list stores Integer objects, not ints, so the compiler rewrites the call as ints.add(Integer.valueOf(42)). Unboxing does the opposite on read.

cards.front: Why can you compute remainder % total on two Integer objects?
cards.extra: The % operator does not apply to objects; the compiler inserts intValue() calls. An unboxing of null throws a NullPointerException.

cards.front: Which wrapper class corresponds to char?
cards.extra: The other wrappers mirror their primitive's name capitalised (int to Integer is the exception). char also has no numeric wrapper shared with int.

cards.front: Which wrapper type is paired with int for autoboxing?
cards.extra: Its siblings mirror the primitive names: Boolean, Long, Double, Float, Short, Byte, Character. Autoboxing maps between each pair implicitly.

cards.front: What is the main benefit of autoboxing and unboxing?
cards.extra: You can mix primitives and their wrappers without explicit conversion calls. The cost, easy to miss, is a hidden allocation per boxed value.

cards.front: Which escape sequence inserts a tab?
cards.extra: Other common escapes are \n for newline, \r for carriage return, \f for form feed and \b for backspace.

cards.front: How do you put a double quote inside a string literal?
cards.extra: Likewise a single quote inside a character literal is \', and a literal backslash is \\. An unescaped interior quote ends the literal.

cards.front: What does a backslash followed by a line terminator do in a string literal?
cards.back: It inserts nothing - the line break is removed
cards.extra: That lets you break a long literal across source lines without adding characters. \s is the opposite trick: it inserts a real space.

cards.front: What does the \s escape sequence insert?
cards.extra: Useful to keep a trailing space that an editor would otherwise trim. It differs from an ordinary space in that it survives formatting tools.

cards.front: What is the type of a Character object's single stored value?
cards.extra: Character wraps exactly one char field. That means it is based on 16-bit code units, so it cannot itself hold a supplementary character.

cards.front: Which Character method tests for a letter?
cards.extra: Its relatives are isDigit() and isWhitespace(). Case tests are isUpperCase() and isLowerCase().

cards.front: Which Character method returns a one-character String?
cards.extra: String.valueOf(char) does the same thing. Beware that passing the resulting char to println with an int argument selects a different overload.

cards.front: What character range can a char hold?
cards.extra: A char is 16 bits, encoded as an unsigned range. Code points above 0xFFFF are supplementary characters and need an int or a surrogate pair.

cards.front: Which Unicode range is called the Basic Multilingual Plane?
cards.extra: The full legal range of code points is U+0000 to U+10FFFF. Everything above 0xFFFF is supplementary and does not fit in a single char.

cards.front: How many char values does a supplementary character need?
cards.extra: Since a char is only 16 bits, characters above U+FFFF are encoded as a high and a low surrogate. A String is therefore UTF-16, not a sequence of code points.

cards.front: How do Character's char methods treat surrogate values?
cards.back: As undefined, so supplementary characters are not supported
cards.extra: Methods taking a char cannot see whole supplementary characters. Overloads taking an int code point are the ones that support all of Unicode.

cards.front: Is Character mutable?
cards.extra: Once created, a Character cannot be changed. That is why the API's case-conversion methods return new values instead of modifying in place.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::09 Strings and Methods

cards.front: Which four subclasses of Number are not part of the primitive wrappers?
cards.extra: The numeric pair serves high-precision calculation; AtomicInteger and AtomicLong serve multi-threaded code. All primitive wrappers also extend Number.

cards.front: What is the range of Math.random()?
cards.extra: To get integers 0 to 9 you multiply by 10 and cast to int. For a series of numbers prefer a java.util.Random instance.

cards.front: What is %n in a format string?
cards.extra: You should always use %n rather than \n in printf/format, so the correct line terminator is emitted on Windows as well as Unix.

cards.front: In a printf format string, what does %d specify?
cards.extra: It is one of many converters, each a letter ending a specifier that begins with %. Flags and width can appear between the two.

cards.front: In a format string, what does the flag , do?
cards.extra: On an English locale it turns 1234567 into 1,234,567. The flag sits between % and the converter, as in %,d.

cards.front: Which format specifier prints the full name of a month?
cards.extra: It is locale-specific and followed by a Date argument. Daily numbers are %td (zero-padded) or %te (unpadded).

cards.front: What does a 0 placeholder in a DecimalFormat pattern mean?
cards.back: A digit, showing zeroes when the value is smaller than the digit count
cards.extra: # is a digit placeholder that shows nothing when absent, so 000000.000 pads while ###,###.### drops leading zeroes.

cards.front: What does the # placeholder in a DecimalFormat pattern do?
cards.back: Holds a digit, but shows nothing when it is absent
cards.extra: That is why ###.### formats 123456.789 as 123,456.789 only if grouping chars are supplied; leading zeroes are dropped.

cards.front: How does DecimalFormat handle more decimal places than its pattern allows?
cards.extra: Formatting discards precision rather than throwing. That makes DecimalFormat unsuitable where exactness is required - consider BigDecimal formatting.

cards.front: What does Math.ceil(d) return?
cards.back: The smallest integer >= the argument, as a double
cards.extra: Its opposite is floor(), the largest integer <= argument. Both return a double even though the value is integral.

cards.front: What does Math.rint(d) return?
cards.back: The integer closest in value to the argument, as a double
cards.extra: Unlike round() it keeps the double type and uses ties-to-even rounding. round() returns long for a double argument, int for a float.

cards.front: How does Math.round(double) differ from Math.rint(double) in return type?
cards.extra: Use round(float) for an int result. The difference matters when you assign the outcome to a variable with a specific numeric type.

cards.front: What do Math.pow and Math.sqrt return?
cards.extra: pow(base, exp) raises the first argument to the second; sqrt(d) takes the square root. Everything in Math is static.

cards.front: Which Math constants represent the natural logarithm base and pi?
cards.extra: They are static final fields, so you can read them without instantiating Math. A static import would let you write just E or PI.

cards.front: What unit do Math.sin, Math.cos and Math.tan expect?
cards.extra: Convert with Math.toRadians(degrees). toDegrees() goes the other way; atan2(y, x) converts rectangular to polar.

cards.front: Which Integer method parses a string in binary, octal or hex?
cards.extra: Radix 2 is binary, 8 octal and 16 hexadecimal. The one-argument parseInt(String) accepts decimal only.

cards.front: Which method returns an Integer object, rather than an int, from a string?
cards.extra: Its overload valueOf(String, int radix) parses with a given base. In contrast parseInt returns a primitive int.

cards.front: Why might you choose a Number object instead of a primitive?
cards.back: To pass it where an object is required, e.g. collections
cards.extra: The other listed reasons are access to MIN_VALUE/MAX_VALUE constants and the conversion helpers between types, strings and number systems.

cards.front: How does StringBuilder differ from String fundamentally?
cards.extra: Every apparent String modification returns a new object. A StringBuilder can be changed in place, which avoids allocating intermediate copies.

cards.front: What is a StringBuilder's capacity?
cards.extra: It is always greater than or equal to length(), and grows automatically when content is appended beyond it.

cards.front: What capacity does new StringBuilder() give?
cards.extra: The capacity is a buffer size, not visible content. length() stays 0 until something is appended.

cards.front: What capacity results from new StringBuilder("Greetings")?
cards.extra: The String constructor keeps the characters and appends 16 empty slots for growth. The no-arg constructor gives just 16.

cards.front: Which constructor creates an empty builder with a chosen initial capacity?
cards.extra: Useful when you can estimate the final size, avoiding repeated reallocation. Passing a capacity of 0 is legal but forces reallocation on the first append.

cards.front: What does setLength(n) do when n is smaller than the current length?
cards.extra: When n is larger than the current length, null characters are appended instead. Either way, length changes without touching capacity.

cards.front: Which methods give StringBuilder capabilities that String lacks?
cards.extra: Both are overloaded for any type: the argument's toString() is used. append adds at the end, insert at a given offset.

cards.front: What range does delete(int start, int end) remove?
cards.extra: This is the same half-open convention as substring. To remove one character only, use deleteCharAt(index).

cards.front: Why must you call toString() to use a String method on a builder?
cards.extra: You cannot call replaceAll on a builder directly. Convert to String, apply the String method, then pass the result back into a new builder.

cards.front: What does println(sb) print for a builder containing "Hi"?
cards.extra: The same applies to any object whose class overrides toString(). Type-formatted output requires an explicit call.

cards.front: How does StringBuffer differ from StringBuilder?
cards.back: Same API, but StringBuffer methods are synchronized
cards.extra: Thread safety costs performance. Unless you truly share the buffer across threads, use StringBuilder.

cards.front: Since which Java SE release is string concatenation usually faster than append-based building?
cards.extra: The compiler's concat strategy was optimised in 9. Earlier, appending many strings to a StringBuilder was generally the faster option.

cards.front: Which two StringBuilder methods replace characters in place?
cards.extra: Together with delete, deleteCharAt and insert, these cover in-place editing that String can only do by allocating a new string.

cards.front: Is the String class mutable?
cards.extra: Methods that seem to modify a string actually create and return a new String. That is why s.trim() without assignment changes nothing.

cards.front: What does charAt(i) return?
cards.back: The character at index i, counting from 0
cards.extra: It returns a char, not a String of length one. Use substring(i, i + 1) if you need a one-character String.

cards.front: What range does substring(beginIndex, endIndex) copy?
cards.extra: Half-open again: substring(11, 15) of a longer string yields four characters. The one-argument overload runs to the end of the string.

cards.front: What do indexOf() and lastIndexOf() return when nothing matches?
cards.extra: Never compare the result to 0 to detect absence, since 0 is a valid match at the start. The boolean alternative contains() avoids this check entirely.

cards.front: Which String method answers "does the text appear at all" as a boolean?
cards.extra: It takes a CharSequence, and String implements that interface, so you can pass a String directly. It does not report the match position.

cards.front: Which string concatenation form also accepts non-String operands?
cards.back: The + operator (concat takes only a String)
cards.extra: With + any non-String is converted by calling its toString(). The concat() method is restricted to String arguments.

cards.front: When you concatenate an object with a String, what gets appended?
cards.extra: That is why "x" + sb works for a StringBuilder: its toString() supplies the characters. A null reference appends the text "null".

cards.front: Which static String method returns a formatted String rather than printing it?
cards.extra: It mirrors printf formatting but gives you a reusable String, instead of writing output once to a stream. The format can itself be a text block.

cards.front: Which method converts a numeric string to a primitive directly?
cards.extra: Primitive returned, so nothing is boxed, which makes it more direct than valueOf(). Each numeric wrapper class provides such a method.

cards.front: Which method converts a numeric string into a wrapper object?
cards.extra: The parseXXXX methods return primitives instead. Choose valueOf when the result must be stored where an object is required, such as a collection.

cards.front: Which method searches for a substring using a regular expression and replaces all matches?
cards.extra: Its sibling replaceFirst replaces only the first match. For a plain literal replacement use replace(CharSequence, CharSequence) instead.

cards.front: What is a text block in Java?
cards.back: A multi-line string literal delimited by triple double quotes
cards.extra: Introduced in Java SE 15. It must start with """ followed by a line terminator, and ends with another """.

cards.front: Starting with which Java SE version are text blocks available?
cards.extra: Before that, a literal could not span lines, so multi-line text had to be assembled with + concatenation between lines.

cards.front: What does trim() remove?
cards.extra: Internal spaces survive. It returns a copy, since strings are immutable. Newer code often prefers strip(), which is Unicode-aware.

cards.front: Which method extracts part of a string into an array of strings?
cards.extra: The argument is a regular expression, not a literal separator, so "." must be escaped as "\.". The optional limit caps the array's size.

cards.front: Which String method copies characters into a supplied char array?
cards.extra: It fills a destination array you provide, rather than returning a new one. That is how the sample palindrome program replaces a manual charAt loop.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: In Java documentation, what is a parameter?
cards.back: A variable in the declaration of a method or constructor
cards.extra: Arguments are the actual values supplied at the call site. The arguments must match the declared parameters in type and order.

cards.front: What is an argument?
cards.back: An actual value passed when a method is invoked
cards.extra: The parameters are only the placeholders in the declaration. Java passes every argument by value, parameters and references alike.

cards.front: How do you declare a method that accepts any number of arguments of one type?
cards.back: Varargs: put ... after the last parameter's type
cards.extra: e.g. void print(String... labels). Inside the method the parameter is treated as an array, and it may be called with zero arguments.

cards.front: Inside a varargs method, what type does the parameter have?
cards.extra: A caller may pass either a sequence of values or one array, and the body treats both identically. The compiler packs loose arguments into an array.

cards.front: Can a varargs parameter have parameters after it?
cards.back: No - it must be the last parameter
cards.extra: Earlier parameters of other types come first, e.g. printf(String format, Object... args). Any fixed parameters must precede the ellipsis.

cards.front: How are primitive arguments passed to a method?
cards.back: By value - changes inside the method are lost on return
cards.extra: The method works on a copy, so the caller's variable is untouched. This is true for every parameter in Java; there is no by-reference passing.

cards.front: If a method reassigns a reference parameter to a new object, does the caller see it?
cards.back: No - the caller still points at the original object
cards.extra: The reference was passed by value, so only the local copy is changed. However, mutating the object it points to is visible.

cards.front: If a method mutates a field of an object passed as a parameter, does the caller see the change?
cards.back: Yes - the same object is being changed
cards.extra: Passing by value copies the reference, not the object, so both point to one instance. This only applies to fields the caller's code can access.

cards.front: When does a parameter name shadow a field?
cards.back: When the parameter has the same name as a field
cards.extra: The simple name then refers to the parameter inside the body, and the field needs this.field. It is conventional only in setters and constructors.

cards.front: Why is shadowing a field with a parameter discouraged outside setters?
cards.extra: Readers cannot tell whether a simple name means the parameter or the field. A requalification bug will silently compile when names collide.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: What is the class body?
cards.back: The code between a class declaration's braces
cards.extra: It contains constructors for new objects, field declarations for state, and methods for behaviour. The class name plus body is the minimal declaration.

cards.front: In a class declaration, which keyword introduces the superclass?
cards.extra: e.g. class MountainBike extends Bicycle. A class may extend one parent only, since Java has single class inheritance.

cards.front: Which keyword introduces the list of interfaces a class implements?
cards.extra: The list is comma-separated and a class may implement many interfaces. It must come after any extends clause.

cards.front: How many classes can one class extend?
cards.back: Exactly one (single inheritance); a class may implement many interfaces
cards.extra: The single-superclass rule avoids multiple state inheritance. Multiple types can still be gained by implementing several interfaces.

cards.front: What are the three components of a field declaration, in order?
cards.back: Zero or more modifiers, the type, then the name
cards.extra: e.g. private int speed;. The modifiers are optional; the type and name never are.

cards.front: Why is it common to make fields private?
cards.back: Encapsulation - only the class itself touches the field directly
cards.extra: Access is then given indirectly through public methods, so the class can change its internal representation without breaking callers.

cards.front: Which modifier restricts a field to its own class only?
cards.extra: public exposes it to all classes. There are exceptions to the simple rule, but that is the baseline for both.

cards.front: Why does the compiler restrict private on a top-level class?
cards.back: Only nested classes may be declared private
cards.extra: A top-level class is a file-level unit; private would make it unusable anywhere. Top-level classes use public or package-private.

cards.front: Must a class name start with a capital letter?
cards.back: No - it is convention, not a rule
cards.extra: The compiler accepts any valid identifier. The same applies to the verb-first convention for method names.

cards.front: Are class names and method names subject to the same identifier rules?
cards.extra: Class names capitalise the first letter; method names begin with a lowercase verb. Breaking the convention does not break the code but hurts readability.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: What are the three parts of Point origin = new Point(23, 94);?
cards.extra: The declaration names a variable of the type. The new operator allocates the object and returns a reference. The constructor then initialises it.

cards.front: What does it mean to "instantiate a class"?
cards.back: To create an object, i.e. an instance of that class
cards.extra: The two phrases are interchangeable. Each such call allocates memory and runs exactly one constructor.

cards.front: Does declaring a reference variable create an object?
cards.extra: You must assign an object, usually with new. Using the variable before then is a compile or runtime error.

cards.front: What does a constructor look like in a declaration?
cards.back: Same name as the class, and no return type
cards.extra: That is how you recognise it, e.g. Point(int x, int y). Giving it a return type would turn it into an ordinary method.

cards.front: What is a no-argument constructor?
cards.back: A constructor that takes no arguments
cards.extra: It is the only constructor many classes need, and it enables new Foo(). It differs from the compiler-generated default only in origin.

cards.front: How does the compiler distinguish overloaded constructors?
cards.back: By the number and types of the arguments
cards.extra: Several constructors may exist, but no two may have the same list. e.g. Rectangle(Point, int, int) against Rectangle(int, int).

cards.front: What does the implicit default constructor call?
cards.extra: Which effectively chains back to Object. If the superclass has no no-arg constructor, the program will not compile.

cards.front: What happens when a class has no explicit superclass?
cards.extra: Object provides a no-arg constructor, so the chain always terminates. That is why every class can be created with a default constructor.

cards.front: Which operator accesses an object's fields from outside its class?
cards.back: The dot operator, after an object reference
cards.extra: e.g. rectangle.width. Inside the class you may use the field's simple name instead.

cards.front: Do two instances of the same class share their instance fields?
cards.back: No - each object has its own copy
cards.extra: So rectangle1.width and rectangle2.width are distinct variables. Only static fields are shared.

cards.front: When is an object eligible for garbage collection?
cards.extra: All references must be gone: dropped by going out of scope, or explicitly set to null. Until then the object is reachable and stays.

cards.front: Do you need to destroy Java objects explicitly?
cards.back: No - the garbage collector deletes unreachable ones
cards.extra: There is no free or delete. The runtime decides when to reclaim memory, so objects may linger after becoming unreachable.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: How does a constructor declaration differ from a method declaration?
cards.back: It uses the class name and has no return type
cards.extra: Apart from those two points it looks like a method: it may take parameters, throw exceptions, and carry access modifiers.

cards.front: Who invokes a constructor?
cards.extra: You never call a constructor like a method on an existing object. new Bicycle(30, 0, 8) both allocates and initialises.

cards.front: Can you declare two constructors with the same parameter types?
cards.extra: Overloading is decided by the number and types of the arguments. Identical lists leave the compiler no way to choose.

cards.front: If you declare any constructor, does the compiler still add the default one?
cards.back: No - it only supplies one when none is declared
cards.extra: So a class with only Bicycle(int, int, int) cannot be created with new Bicycle(). Add a no-arg constructor yourself if you need it.

cards.front: What does the compiler-generated default constructor do?
cards.extra: Nothing else, not even field initialisers beyond the normal rules. If the superclass has no no-arg constructor, compilation fails.

cards.front: Why would a class fail to compile if it has no constructors and its superclass has no no-arg constructor?
cards.back: The implicit default constructor has no super constructor to call
cards.extra: The compiler must either call super() or a parameterised form you declare explicitly. Declaring a constructor fixes this.

cards.front: Can a constructor's access modifier restrict who can create objects?
cards.back: Yes - a private constructor blocks outside instantiation
cards.extra: That is the basis of singletons and utility classes. Protected or package-private constructors let only certain callers build the object.

cards.front: How can a subclass constructor reuse its superclass's constructor?
cards.back: Call super(args) as the constructor's first action
cards.extra: With no explicit call the compiler inserts super(). That start-of-constructor restriction was loosened starting with JDK 25.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: Which six components make up a full method declaration, in order?
cards.back: Modifiers, return type, name, parameter list, exception list, body
cards.extra: Only the return type, name, parentheses and body are strictly required: the rest may be omitted from the declaration.

cards.front: What is a method's signature?
cards.extra: Return type, modifiers and exception declarations are not part of it. Overloading is resolved by the signature alone.

cards.front: What does the return type void mean?
cards.extra: A return; statement is still allowed to exit early. A non-void method must return a value of the declared type.

cards.front: Since when do method names have to begin with a lowercase verb?
cards.back: It is a convention, not a language rule
cards.extra: Any legal identifier compiles, though the convention is universally expected. Multi-word names capitalise each later word, e.g. getBalance.

cards.front: What is method overloading?
cards.back: Several methods in one class sharing a name but with different parameter lists
cards.extra: The compiler distinguishes them by the number and types of the arguments. They can differ in return type only if the parameters differ too.

cards.front: Does the return type participate in deciding which overload applies?
cards.extra: Two methods with the same name and parameters but different return types is a compile error. The compiler cannot tell which the call intends.

cards.front: Can two methods share a name if one differs only in return type?
cards.extra: An overload must change the parameter list. Return type is not part of the signature used for telling methods apart.

cards.front: Why should overloading be used sparingly?
cards.back: Too many same-named variants make code less readable
cards.extra: Callers cannot tell at a glance which overload runs, and a subtle argument conversion can silently pick a different one.

cards.front: If a class has draw(String), may it add draw(int)?
cards.back: Yes - distinct parameter types make them valid overloads
cards.extra: This is preferable to inventing drawString/drawInteger names, since one name expresses one concept and the compiler picks by type.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: When should you choose a local class?
cards.back: When you need more than one instance, its constructor, or a named type
cards.extra: It also earns its keep when you want to call additional methods later. A one-shot instance instead calls for an anonymous class or a lambda.

cards.front: When should you choose an anonymous class?
cards.back: When you need to declare fields or additional methods
cards.extra: You get exactly one unnamed instance of the class, created at the expression's site. That is why a constructor is forbidden.

cards.front: When should you choose a lambda expression?
cards.back: When it encapsulates a single unit of behaviour to pass along
cards.extra: Alternatively, when a simple instance of a functional interface suffices and you need no fields, constructor or extra methods.

cards.front: When should you choose a nested class over a local class?
cards.back: When the type should be more widely available and needs no local variables
cards.extra: A nested class is a member of the enclosing class, so other code can use it, whereas a local class exists only inside its block.

cards.front: When must you use a non-static (inner) nested class rather than a static one?
cards.back: When you need access to an enclosing instance's non-public members
cards.extra: Otherwise choose a static nested class, which has no implicit outer instance and is therefore simpler and leak-free.

cards.front: Why is a lambda often preferred to an anonymous class for a one-method callback?
cards.back: It states just the behaviour, with no boilerplate class
cards.extra: Anonymous classes are still needed when you declare fields or extra methods. Otherwise the lambda's brevity wins and reads more clearly.

cards.front: Which construct gives you exactly one unnamed instance and no constructor?
cards.extra: It is an expression, so the instance is created where it is written and can never be created again or from elsewhere. That matches helper objects used once.

cards.front: What is an enum?
cards.back: A class whose instances are fixed and known to the compiler
cards.extra: You list them as enum constants in the body, separated by commas. No other instances can be created.

cards.front: Which class do all enums implicitly extend?
cards.extra: Because the superclass is fixed, an enum cannot extend another class. It also cannot be subclassed: enums are effectively final.

cards.front: Which method returns the name of an enum constant?
cards.extra: It returns exactly the identifier as declared, which matters when persisting values. toString() may be overridden, name() cannot.

cards.front: What does ordinal() return?
cards.back: The constant's position in the declaration, starting at 0
cards.extra: The first constant has ordinal 0. That ordering is also enums' default natural ordering for Comparable.

cards.front: Which static method returns all enum instances?
cards.extra: It returns an array in declaration order. valueOf(String) does the reverse, and both are added implicitly by the compiler.

cards.front: What does valueOf(String) do?
cards.back: Returns the instance whose name matches the argument
cards.extra: It matches the identifier exactly and is case-sensitive. An unknown name causes an IllegalArgumentException.

cards.front: How do you add a constructor, field or method to an enum?
cards.back: List the constants, add a semicolon, then declare the members
cards.extra: The ; is mandatory before any member declarations. Without it the compiler keeps expecting more constants.

cards.front: How are constructor arguments supplied to an enum constant?
cards.extra: e.g. MONDAY("Monday"). The arguments are passed to the enum's (implicitly private) constructor.

cards.front: What ensures a switch expression handles every enum constant?
cards.back: Compile-time exhaustiveness checking (missing value is an error)
cards.extra: The compiler rejects a switch expression that lacks a branch for a constant. Sealed classes plus pattern matching bring the same guarantee to regular classes.

cards.front: How does an enum with a single constant implement the singleton pattern?
cards.back: The one constant is the only instance
cards.extra: It is thread-safe, lazily class-initialised, and resistant to reflection and serialisation creating more instances.

cards.front: Can an enum declare abstract methods?
cards.extra: The enum itself cannot be extended, but the constants behave like implicit subclasses. That is the template-method style often used for per-constant behaviour.

cards.front: What breaks when an enum constant is removed or added while code persists or switches on it?
cards.back: Compilation errors, silent defaults, or stale persisted values
cards.extra: A stored ordinal or name can no longer resolve. Review every use site, and prefer storing the name over the ordinal.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: Why do you write this.x = x; in a constructor?
cards.back: The parameter shadows the field, so this.x names the field
cards.extra: Without the qualifier the assignment would copy the parameter onto itself. This pattern appears only when names collide.

cards.front: What is an explicit constructor invocation?
cards.back: Calling one constructor of the class from another with this(...)
cards.extra: It centralises initialisation logic: the simple constructors delegate to the most complete one. Before JDK 25 it had to be the first statement.

cards.front: Which access modifier allows access from the same package and from subclasses in other packages?
cards.extra: It is broader than package-private, which allows subclasses nowhere outside the package. It is narrower than public.

cards.front: Which access modifier gives access only within the same package?
cards.extra: Package-private members are not visible to subclasses in other packages. It is the default when you write no modifier.

cards.front: Which access level should you choose for a member?
cards.back: The most restrictive one that makes sense (usually private)
cards.extra: Wider access ties callers to implementation details and limits future change. Public fields in particular should be avoided.

cards.front: What does the static modifier do to a field?
cards.back: Makes it a class variable, shared by every instance
cards.extra: There is exactly one copy, in one memory location, and any instance can read or change it. Constant-like aggregates or counters live here.

cards.front: How should a class (static) variable be referenced?
cards.extra: Referencing it through an instance reference compiles but is discouraged, because it obscures that the field is shared.

cards.front: Can a static method access instance fields directly?
cards.back: No - it needs an object reference, or it must use static members
cards.extra: There is no instance when a static method runs, so this is not available either. This keeps static methods free of implicit state.

cards.front: Why is final needed on top of static to define a constant?
cards.back: static alone leaves the value mutable; final prohibits reassignment
cards.extra: e.g. static final double PI = 3.141592653589793;. Reassigning it afterwards is a compile-time error.

cards.front: Which naming convention applies to constants?
cards.extra: MAX_SPEED, not maxSpeed. The uppercase signal from the declaration tells readers the value cannot change.

cards.front: When are static initialization blocks executed?
cards.back: In source order, when the class is initialised
cards.extra: A class may have several, placed anywhere in the body. They run once, before any instance exists.

cards.front: Why can't a failing static initializer be retried?
cards.back: It runs at most once - a failure leaves the class unusable
cards.extra: If the block touches a missing file or network resource and throws, the class is never initialised, and no instance can be created.

cards.front: What is the advantage of a private static method over a static initialization block?
cards.back: It can be reused to reinitialise the class variable later
cards.extra: A static block is a one-shot, non-reentrant action. A method can be called again for a reset, which a block can never do.

cards.front: How does a final method help with instance initialization?
cards.back: Being final, it cannot be overridden while the object is being constructed
cards.extra: Subclass overrides would run against a partially built object. Making the init method final prevents that trap.

cards.front: Can an interface name be used as a return type?
cards.back: Yes - the returned object must implement that interface
cards.extra: This is what makes polymorphic factories possible: callers program against the interface and need not know the concrete class.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::05 Nested Classes

cards.front: What is a nested class?
cards.extra: It is divided into two kinds: non-static nested classes, called inner classes, and static nested classes.

cards.front: What is a non-static nested class called?
cards.extra: It is tied to an instance of the enclosing class, and its objects each exist within such an instance.

cards.front: What is the difference between an inner class and a static nested class in access?
cards.back: An inner class sees all enclosing members; a static one only via a reference
cards.extra: Inner classes reach even private fields and methods of the enclosing instance. Static nested classes have no implicit enclosing instance.

cards.front: Which access modifiers may a nested class have?
cards.extra: Outer top-level classes can only be public or package-private, because a file has no notion of private classes.

cards.front: Why can't a top-level class be declared private?
cards.back: It has no enclosing class to hide it from
cards.extra: A file-level type must be reachable from its own file or package, so only public and package-private apply. Private is reserved for nested classes.

cards.front: How is an instance of an inner class created?
cards.back: First instantiate the outer class; then use outerObj.new InnerClass()
cards.extra: Writing new OuterClass.InnerClass() instead is a compile error. The inner instance needs an outer instance to belong to.

cards.front: How is a static nested class instantiated?
cards.back: Exactly like a top-level class, e.g. new Outer.StaticNested()
cards.extra: No outer instance is needed. Behaviourally, the static nested class is a top-level class nested only for packaging convenience.

cards.front: Why can a static nested class not use the enclosing class's instance field directly?
cards.extra: It reaches the field only through an object reference, exactly as any other class would have to.

cards.front: What is a local class?
cards.back: A class declared inside a block, typically a method body
cards.extra: Its visibility is restricted to that block. It may be declared in a loop or an if clause, not only in a method.

cards.front: Which local variables can a local class access?
cards.extra: Since Java SE 8, effectively final is enough. A variable counts as effectively final if it is never reassigned after initialisation.

cards.front: What does a local class do when it uses an enclosing local variable?
cards.extra: That is why the variable must not later change: the class keeps a copy. Reassigning it would make the captured value diverge from the source.

cards.front: Can a local class declare a static method?
cards.back: No, unless it is a constant variable
cards.extra: A local class may hold static members only if they are compile-time constants. Interfaces declared inside a block are also rejected, since they are inherently static.

cards.front: In a static method, which enclosing members can a local class use?
cards.extra: There is no instance to draw on. A non-static field of the enclosing class therefore cannot be referenced from such a class.

cards.front: How does an anonymous class differ from a local class?
cards.back: No name - it is an expression, not a declaration
cards.extra: It is limited to a single-use helper. Being an expression, it carries its semicolon and appears right where the object is needed.

cards.front: Can an anonymous class declare a constructor?
cards.back: No - it has no name to give one
cards.extra: Fields, extra methods, instance initializers and nested classes are all fine. Instance initializers are the usual substitute for constructor code.

cards.front: Why is serialising inner classes discouraged?
cards.extra: Serialised bytes from one JRE may not deserialize under another. Synthetic constructs let compilers add language features without changing the JVM.

cards.front: What is an abstract class?
cards.back: A class that cannot be instantiated, but can be subclassed
cards.extra: It may or may not declare abstract methods. Its code acts as a partial implementation shared by subclasses.

cards.front: What is an abstract method?
cards.back: A method declared with no body, ending in a semicolon
cards.extra: Subclasses must implement it, or they too must be declared abstract. It exists to force a type-specific implementation.

cards.front: If a class declares any abstract method, what must be true of the class?
cards.extra: abstract void draw(); in a concrete class is a compile error. The abstract modifier cannot be omitted.

cards.front: What must a subclass do with inherited abstract methods?
cards.back: Implement all of them, or be declared abstract itself
cards.extra: This is the enforcement mechanism: a subclass that forgets one cannot be created until the hole is filled.

cards.front: Can an abstract class have concrete methods and non-static fields?
cards.back: Yes - unlike interfaces it may hold both
cards.extra: Abstract classes may have shared state and protected or private concrete methods. That is the main reason to pick one over an interface.

cards.front: Can an abstract class have static fields and static methods?
cards.extra: Static members are not subject to the abstract-instantiation rule. They are shared like the statics of any other class.

cards.front: What are interface fields implicitly?
cards.extra: That means interfaces cannot hold mutable state, which removes multiple-inheritance-of-state problems. Abstract classes may, so a class extending one can share state.

cards.front: Can a class implement several interfaces but extend only one class?
cards.extra: Single inheritance of class avoids conflicting state; many interfaces supply multiple types. Interfaces may also extend several interfaces.

cards.front: When is an abstract class a better fit than an interface?
cards.back: When related classes must share code, common fields, or non-public helpers
cards.extra: Interfaces suit unrelated implementors and pure type contracts. An abstract superclass can hold reusable state and behaviour.

cards.front: When is an interface a better fit than an abstract class?
cards.back: When unrelated classes should implement the same type or behaviour
cards.extra: e.g. Comparable and Cloneable span unrelated hierarchies. And a class may implement several interfaces, giving multiple type inheritance.

cards.front: Which abstract class provides the shared map implementation for HashMap and TreeMap?
cards.extra: Its subclasses inherit ready-made get, put and isEmpty. Mutable shared code is exactly what an interface could not provide.

cards.front: Which JDK class demonstrates one class mixing interfaces with an abstract superclass?
cards.extra: HashMap implements Map, Cloneable and Serializable, and also extends AbstractMap. Its interfaces advertise its contract; the abstract class supplies shared code.

cards.front: Can an abstract class implement only some methods of an interface?
cards.back: Yes - that is why it must be abstract
cards.extra: A concrete subclass then implements the rest. An interface cannot be declared abstract, so only classes can carry the obligation forward.

cards.front: Why is an abstract class with a draw() abstract method useful for shapes?
cards.back: Shared state and logic live in one place, while each shape supplies its own drawing
cards.extra: Position, colour and moveTo() are inherited once. What differs per subclass stays abstract, so the compiler forces each shape to implement it.

cards.front: Which class sits at the top of every hierarchy?
cards.extra: Every class is a direct or indirect descendant. It supplies the contract: equals, hashCode, toString, getClass and more.

cards.front: What does the Object version of equals() do?
cards.extra: Two distinct Book objects with the same ISBN are unequal until you override equals. Override it whenever identity is not the right notion of equality.

cards.front: If you override equals(), what else must you override?
cards.extra: Objects equal by equals must have equal hash codes. Otherwise a HashSet or HashMap lookup can miss a key that is present.

cards.front: What does getClass() return, and can it be overridden?
cards.back: The runtime Class object; it cannot be overridden
cards.extra: It is final. The returned Class exposes getSimpleName, getSuperclass, getInterfaces and many other reflective queries.

cards.front: What does clone() require of a class?
cards.extra: Otherwise the call throws CloneNotSupportedException. Adding implements Cloneable lets Object.clone make a shallow copy.

cards.front: Is Object.clone() a deep or shallow copy?
cards.back: Shallow - member references are copied, not the objects they point to
cards.extra: If a member references an external object, original and clone share it, so a change is visible in both. Override clone to also copy such members.

cards.front: Why should you not rely on finalize() for cleanup?
cards.back: It may never be called, or when it runs is uncertain
cards.extra: As of Java SE 18 it is deprecated for removal. Use AutoCloseable plus try-with-resources for deterministic release.

cards.front: Which interface should replace finalize() for resource cleanup?
cards.extra: Its close() runs deterministically via try-with-resources, rather than at the JVM's whim. This frees resources when the block exits.

cards.front: Why override toString() in your own classes?
cards.back: To give objects a useful text representation for debugging and logging
cards.extra: The inherited version prints a class name and a hash hex. A good override shows the real state, which is what appears inside string concatenation.

cards.front: Which three methods of Object support thread synchronisation?
cards.extra: They coordinate independently running threads. All must be called while holding the object's monitor.

cards.front: What is required to override an instance method?
cards.back: Same signature (name and parameter types) and same or covariant return type
cards.extra: The overriding method may narrow the return type to a subtype. That narrower type is called a covariant return type.

cards.front: What does the @Override annotation do?
cards.back: Tells the compiler you intend to override, and errors if nothing is overridden
cards.extra: It turns a silent typo in the method name into a compile error. Using it is recommended on every override.

cards.front: What happens when a subclass declares a static method with the same signature as a superclass static method?
cards.back: The subclass method hides the superclass one
cards.extra: Hiding is not overriding. Which version runs depends on the static type used for the call, not on the object.

cards.front: Why is that difference between overriding and hiding significant?
cards.back: Overrides dispatch on the object; hidden statics on the type
cards.extra: So Animal.testClassMethod() runs Animal's static, while an instance call runs Cat's override. Resolution of statics happens at compile time.

cards.front: When a subclass declares an instance method matching a superclass static method, what happens?
cards.extra: Instance and static cannot be mixed for the same signature. The reverse (static in subclass, instance in superclass) is also an error.

cards.front: Can an overriding method reduce the visibility of the overridden method?
cards.back: No - it may widen it, not narrow it
cards.extra: A protected method can become public, but not private. Narrowing would break callers who compiled against the broader access.

cards.front: When do two interface default methods with the same signature cause an error?
cards.back: When they are independently defined or conflict with an abstract method
cards.extra: The compiler refuses to guess; the class must override the method. Overridden or inherited-from-a-common-ancestor methods are excluded from the conflict.

cards.front: If a superclass instance method clashes with an interface default method, which wins?
cards.extra: Instance methods are preferred over interface defaults. In the horse/Dragon examples, the class's own method silently takes precedence.

cards.front: How do you call a specific interface's default implementation from a class?
cards.extra: The name before super must be a direct superinterface that defines or inherits that default. This also works to reach a class's default.

cards.front: Are static methods in interfaces inherited by implementing classes?
cards.extra: They belong to the interface and are called as Interface.method(). Default methods, by contrast, are inherited normally.

cards.front: What does a subclass do if it declares a new method with the same name but different parameters?
cards.extra: It is a new, distinct method in the subclass, unique to it. Parent classes are unaffected.

cards.front: What does polymorphism let a subclass do?
cards.back: Share the parent's interface while defining its own behaviour
cards.extra: The subclass overrides methods but is still usable wherever the parent type is expected, so callers code to one type.

cards.front: Which method does the JVM call when an overridden method is invoked through a superclass variable?
cards.back: The object's version, not the variable's declared type
cards.extra: This is virtual method invocation and the core of polymorphism. Which method runs is decided from the runtime class of the object.

cards.front: What is field hiding?
cards.back: A subclass field with the same name as a superclass field
cards.extra: Fields are not polymorphic, so the declared type decides which is read. Hiding fields is discouraged because it makes code hard to follow.

cards.front: How do you reach a hidden superclass field from a subclass?
cards.extra: The simple name picks the subclass's field, since that declaration shadows the other. Hiding is discouraged for exactly this confusion.

cards.front: How do you call a superclass method you have overridden?
cards.extra: useful as "call the parent's logic" in combination with extra work. Without super the call would recurse into the override.

cards.front: How is a superclass constructor called from a subclass constructor?
cards.extra: super() calls the no-arg constructor; super(list) the matching one. If neither is present, the compiler inserts super() implicitly.

cards.front: What happens if a constructor does not explicitly call super()?
cards.back: The compiler inserts a call to the superclass's no-arg constructor
cards.extra: so a superclass lacking a no-arg constructor breaks compilation. Object has one, which is why bare classes always work.

cards.front: What is constructor chaining?
cards.back: The implicit chain of superclass constructors up to Object
cards.extra: Every constructor runs along the chain, so some code runs once per level. With long hierarchies, this matters for correctness and performance.

cards.front: What does final on a method prohibit?
cards.extra: Use it on methods whose behaviour must not change, particularly those central to a consistent object state. Object declares several final methods.

cards.front: Why should methods called from constructors be final?
cards.back: A non-final method can be overridden and run against a half-built object
cards.extra: The override executes before the subclass's fields are initialised, so it sees defaults. A final method avoids the surprising result.

cards.front: What does declaring an entire class final do?
cards.extra: Useful for immutable value types; String is the prime example. It also guarantees no subclass can change the behaviour.

cards.front: Can a superclass constructor call with no no-arg constructor still compile?
cards.extra: The implicit super() has nothing to bind to, so you must call an explicit super(args) in the subclass constructor.

cards.front: What is a superclass?
cards.back: The class a subclass is derived from (base or parent class)
cards.extra: A subclass is the derived (extended) class. Members of the superclass, apart from constructors, are inherited.

cards.front: How many direct superclasses does a class have?
cards.extra: This is single inheritance of classes. Multiple inheritance of type instead comes from implementing several interfaces.

cards.front: If no superclass is given, what is a class's implicit parent?
cards.extra: So every class is an Object and inherits its methods. The inheritance chain always terminates at Object.

cards.front: Are constructors inherited?
cards.back: No - but the superclass constructor can be invoked from a subclass
cards.extra: Constructors are not members, so a subclass does not inherit them. It calls one with super(...).

cards.front: Which members does a subclass inherit from its parent?
cards.back: All public and protected members, plus package-private in-package ones
cards.extra: It never inherits private members, regardless of package. Package-private members vanish once the subclass lives elsewhere.

cards.front: What can a subclass do with inherited members?
cards.back: Use them as-is, replace them, hide them, or supplement them
cards.extra: Use, override (instance methods), hide (fields or static methods), or add new members. All four are legal; only hiding fields is discouraged.

cards.front: Does a subclass inherit its parent's private members?
cards.extra: It can still reach them indirectly, through public or protected methods the parent provides. A nested class, by contrast, sees the enclosing class's private members.

cards.front: What is implicit casting in an inheritance context?
cards.back: Assigning a subclass reference to a superclass variable without a cast
cards.extra: e.g. Object obj = new MountainBike();. Legal because a MountainBike is a Bicycle and an Object.

cards.front: Which operator guards a downcast against a runtime failure?
cards.extra: Check the type first, then cast safely, since a failed cast throws. Pattern matching for instanceof folds the check and the declaration into one step.

cards.front: What type of multiple inheritance does Java allow?
cards.back: Of type - many interfaces, but only one superclass
cards.extra: A class implementing several interfaces has several types. State and implementation inheritance through many classes are excluded to avoid ambiguity.

cards.front: Why does Java forbid multiple inheritance of state?
cards.back: The same field could be defined twice, with no rule to pick
cards.extra: Interfaces have no fields (only constants), so implementing many cannot duplicate state. Default methods are one exception handled by explicit compiler rules.

cards.front: What is a Java interface?
cards.back: A reference type of constants and method signatures (plus defaults)
cards.extra: It cannot be instantiated, only implemented by classes or extended by other interfaces. The signatures have no braces, so the implementing classes supply the bodies.

cards.front: What is a default method in an interface?
cards.back: A method with the default modifier and a body
cards.extra: It lets you add functionality to a published interface without breaking implementors, since they inherit the body instead of implementing it.

cards.front: What is the implicit access level of an interface method?
cards.extra: You may omit the keyword, and you cannot narrow it. Fields are implicitly public static final.

cards.front: What is the implicit modifier set of an interface constant?
cards.extra: Constants may be declared without any modifiers. Mutable state is impossible, which is why interfaces avoid the state-inheritance problem.

cards.front: Can an interface have private methods?
cards.back: Yes, since Java SE 9 - to share code among the interface's own defaults
cards.extra: They belong to the implementation, are not callable from outside, and can be neither default nor abstract. They also cannot be protected.

cards.front: Can an interface have protected methods?
cards.extra: Allowed are public members, private instance methods, and private or public static methods. A protected interface method is a compile error.

cards.front: How many interfaces can one interface extend?
cards.extra: Unlike classes, which may extend only one class. This is how the type system supports multiple inheritance of type.

cards.front: What happens to a non-public interface?
cards.back: It is accessible only to classes in the same package
cards.extra: Declaring it public opens it to any class in any package. Without the modifier, it is package-private.

cards.front: Which keyword do implementing classes use, and where must it appear?
cards.extra: The list is comma-separated and may name several interfaces, e.g. extends A implements B, C.

cards.front: What does an implementing class have to supply for each abstract interface method?
cards.extra: An abstract class is exempt, at the price of not being instantiable. A concrete class missing one body will not compile.

cards.front: Why are interfaces described as contracts?
cards.back: They specify how software parts interact, not how either is implemented
cards.extra: Producers can publish an interface, and consumers program against it. Each side can change its internals as long as the contract holds.

cards.front: What role does an interface play when it is published as an API?
cards.back: The public signatures, with the implementation hidden
cards.extra: The vendor may reimplement freely as long as the published interface continues to be implemented. Callers only need the interface to compile and run.

cards.front: Where does the implements clause go in a class declaration?
cards.back: After the extends clause, if one is present
cards.extra: It may list several interfaces, separated by commas. You cannot put a superclass after it.

cards.front: Why would two unrelated classes implement the same interface such as Relatable?
cards.back: So code written against the interface can compare any of them
cards.extra: A findLargest(Relatable, Relatable) method then works for rectangles, books or students. The method needs no knowledge of each class.

cards.front: In isLargerThan(Relatable other), why is a cast to the concrete class needed?
cards.back: The parameter's type is Relatable; subclass members are not visible
cards.extra: You must cast to RectanglePlus to call getArea(). The compiler does not know the interface reference is a RectanglePlus.

cards.front: What breaks if you add an abstract method to a published interface?
cards.extra: Each must now supply the new method, so source-incompatible changes break clients. This is why interface evolution is deliberate.

cards.front: How can you add a method to an interface without breaking implementors?
cards.back: Declare it default with an implementation body
cards.extra: Existing implementors inherit the body unchanged and need no recompilation. Adding a new static method has the same compatibility property.

cards.front: What is the alternative to adding the method to the existing interface?
cards.back: Publish a new interface that extends it
