cards.extra: e.g. DoItPlus extends DoIt. Users may stay on the old interface or upgrade, giving them a choice rather than a forced migration.

cards.front: How does a class express a default-method override to call the interface version?
cards.extra: Needed when two default methods clash and the class must pick one. Without the override, the compiler rejects the ambiguity.

cards.front: If two implemented interfaces define conflicting default methods, what must the class do?
cards.extra: The compiler refuses to choose for you. Inside the override, call whichever defaults with the InterfaceName.super form.

cards.front: Why was the Comparator interface enhanced with comparing and thenComparing?
cards.back: To let callers build comparators from criteria, not whole classes
cards.extra: Previously each sort order demanded a Comparator implementation. Now method references and chained calls express the ordering declaratively.

cards.front: What does the thenComparing default method do?
cards.extra: Its Function overload extracts a Comparable key. The Int/Long/Double variants avoid boxing and unboxing that key.

cards.front: What does Comparator.reversed() do?
cards.back: Returns a comparator with the opposite order
cards.extra: Inverting an existing comparator replaces writing a fresh lambda. Chain it last, as in comparing(...).reversed().

cards.front: Which static method builds a comparator from a key-extraction function?
cards.extra: It uses the returned key's natural order. Siblings are comparingInt, comparingLong and comparingDouble.

cards.front: When an interface gains a default method, do implementing classes need to recompile?
cards.back: No, as long as no other interface they implement clashes
cards.extra: Binary compatibility is the whole point. The new methods can even accept lambda expressions as parameters.

cards.front: When you define an interface, what are you also defining?
cards.extra: Its name is usable anywhere a type name can appear, e.g. as a variable type, parameter or return type.

cards.front: If a variable's type is an interface, what may be assigned to it?
cards.back: Only instances of classes that implement it
cards.extra: An unrelated class cannot. That is how types like Comparable become a guarantee of behaviour across unrelated hierarchies.

cards.front: How can a method accept "anything comparable" without knowing its class?
cards.back: Declare the parameter as the interface, e.g. Relatable
cards.extra: Only the interface's methods are callable on the parameter. A common filter is that both operands must be of the same class.

cards.front: Why does programming to an interface give some of the benefits of multiple inheritance?
cards.back: An object has its own class type plus every implemented interface type
cards.extra: So it can be passed to code expecting the superclass and to code expecting the interface, taking behaviour from both.

cards.front: What is a package?
cards.back: A grouping of related types providing access protection and namespace management
cards.extra: Types here means classes, interfaces, enums and annotation types. Same-named types can live in different packages without collision.

cards.front: Where must a package statement appear in a source file?
cards.back: As the first line of the file
cards.extra: Only one such statement is allowed, and it applies to every type in the file. An import would have to come after it.

cards.front: How many public types may a source file declare?
cards.back: One, and the file must be named after it
cards.extra: Non-public (package-private) types may share the file, though that is discouraged. They will not be accessible outside the package.

cards.front: Where do types end up if the source file has no package statement?
cards.extra: Appropriate only for small or temporary code. The unnamed package itself cannot be imported from a named package in modern Java.

cards.front: What is the fully qualified name of Rectangle declared in package graphics?
cards.extra: It is the type's simple name prefixed by its package. The same class name can also exist as java.awt.Rectangle.

cards.front: What naming convention applies to package names?
cards.extra: This avoids clashing with class or interface names. A capitalised package would look like a type to readers.

cards.front: How do companies name packages to keep them globally unique?
cards.back: Start with their reversed Internet domain, e.g. com.example.mypackage
cards.extra: Domain registration guarantees uniqueness. Name collisions inside a company can be broken up with a region or project segment.

cards.front: Which packages are implicitly imported into every source file?
cards.extra: That is why String and System need no import. Everything else must be imported or fully qualified.

cards.front: What does import graphics.*; import?
cards.extra: The wildcard does not reach graphics.color or graphics.font. Those must be imported separately.

cards.front: Can * in an import statement match a subset of types?
cards.back: No - only a whole package; a prefix form is a compile error
cards.extra: The wildcard means every type in the named package, one level only. To pull in named nested classes, import them explicitly instead.

cards.front: Is java.awt.color a member of the java.awt package?
cards.back: No - they are separate packages that share a prefix
cards.extra: Packages only look hierarchical; the dot is part of the name. Importing java.awt.* therefore does not bring in java.awt.color.

cards.front: When two imported packages contain a type with the same simple name, what must you do?
cards.back: Use its fully qualified name to disambiguate
cards.extra: Both graphics.Rectangle and java.awt.Rectangle are visible, so the simple name is ambiguous and the compiler rejects it.

cards.front: What does a static import let you omit?
cards.back: The class name prefix on static members, e.g. of Math
cards.extra: You may import one member (import static java.lang.Math.PI;) or all (import static java.lang.Math.*;).

cards.front: How should static imports be used?
cards.extra: Overuse hides where a static object comes from, hurting readability. Used narrowly, they remove repetitive class-name prefixes.

cards.front: What does Java reflection let an object discover about itself?
cards.extra: Reflection can also read and write fields, invoke methods and call constructors to create objects. All of this happens at runtime.

cards.front: Which class is the entry point for all reflection?
cards.extra: It models a runtime type and offers members, constructors and annotations. It is itself a subclass of Object.

cards.front: What does obj.getClass() return?
cards.back: The actual implementation class of the object
cards.extra: The declared type of the variable is ignored: a Set variable holding a HashSet returns HashSet. The method is inherited from Object and is final.

cards.front: How do you get a Class object when you have no instance?
cards.extra: It works for types that cannot be instantiated, such as interfaces and primitives. List.class is legal and needs no object.

cards.front: How do you load a class whose name is only known as a String at runtime?
cards.extra: The name must be fully qualified. If the class does not exist, the call throws ClassNotFoundException.

cards.front: Which class loader holds the JDK's own classes?
cards.extra: Its class loader appears as null when queried. Your own classes load in the system, that is application, class loader.

cards.front: Why does launching with java Foo.java instead of java Foo matter for reflection?
cards.back: The two modes use different class loaders
cards.extra: In single-file source mode a memory class loader is used, otherwise the application class loader. Classes in separate loaders are invisible to each other.

cards.front: Which exception type covers everything that can go wrong with a reflective call?
cards.extra: It wraps NoSuchMethodException, IllegalAccessException and related failures. Catching it avoids a long list of catch clauses.

cards.front: What does a NoSuchMethodException indicate?
cards.back: No method matching the name and parameter types was found
cards.extra: The lookup matches types strictly, so boxing and generic erasure are frequent causes of a method seeming to disappear.

cards.front: When invoking a static method reflectively, what is the first argument to invoke()?
cards.extra: There is no receiver object for a static method. Passing any other object is an error.

cards.front: What does deep reflection mean?
cards.extra: It can even change a private final field. Converting a class to a record blocks that, since record fields cannot be mutated.

cards.front: Why must deep reflection be authorised by the module system?
cards.back: Deep reflection needs the package to be opened to your module
cards.extra: By default a named module is closed, so other modules and the unnamed module cannot reach non-public members. --add-opens works but is a last resort.

cards.front: Why does the article warn against deep reflection into a library's internals?
cards.back: The library may rename or retype fields, breaking your code
cards.extra: Opening a package gives unfettered access to implementation details. A field rename becomes a runtime failure with no compile-time warning.

cards.front: Why avoid running code with java Foo.java when it relies on another compiled class?
cards.back: The two classes end up in different class loaders
cards.extra: Then instanceof and casting fail confusingly. Compile both classes and run them from the classpath instead.

cards.front: What is a method handle?
cards.back: A directly invocable reference to a method, constructor or field
cards.extra: It is a low-level mechanism for lookup and invocation, and it can be adapted: arguments reordered, inserted, filtered or return values transformed.

cards.front: How does method-handle access checking differ from reflection's?
cards.back: Checked once, when the handle is created, not per call
cards.extra: That is why method-handle invocation is faster than reflection. The cost is that a leaked handle can expose what it points at.

cards.front: Why must method handles be kept private if they reach non-public members?
cards.back: Whatever they can reach, their holders can reach too
cards.extra: The check is at creation, so passing the handle on passes the privilege. Build them with a restricted Lookup when they must escape.

cards.front: Which factory creates method handles?
cards.extra: You decide its access level when creating it. A private lookup can find private members of the class it is created in.

cards.front: How do you make a Lookup that can only find public members?
cards.extra: It searches public members of public classes in unconditionally exported packages only. That is the safe option for handles you hand to other code.

cards.front: Which class describes a method handle's type?
cards.extra: Instantiate it with the return type first, then all argument types: methodType(String.class, char.class, char.class).

cards.front: Which Lookup method finds an instance method?
cards.extra: It takes the class, the method name as a String and a MethodType. findStatic is the counterpart for static methods.

cards.front: What does MethodHandle.invokeExact require?
cards.back: The arguments must strictly match the handle's type
cards.extra: Any mismatch fails at runtime with a wrong-type error. It is the fastest path but the least forgiving.

cards.front: What does MethodHandle.invoke do differently from invokeExact?
cards.back: It adapts types to match (asType) before invoking exactly
cards.extra: It is more permissive and slightly slower. It accepts Objects and converts them to the handle's parameter types.

cards.front: What does invokeWithArguments accept that invoke does not?
cards.back: All the arguments as a single array or list of objects
cards.extra: Extra arguments beyond the expected count are squashed into the final array parameter. That suits varargs targets.

cards.front: Why are VarHandles preferred over field method handles?
cards.back: They support atomic and ordered memory access, and are the modern API
cards.extra: Field handles still work, but are unusual for field access. VarHandles are created with findVarHandle and findStaticVarHandle.

cards.front: Which exception must a method that invokes a handle declare or catch?
cards.extra: Both invokeExact and invoke throw Throwable, since the underlying method may throw anything. Neither is usable without handling it.

cards.front: What does MethodHandles.catchException wrap?
cards.back: A target handle plus a handler handle for one exception type
cards.extra: The handler must return the same type as the target and take the Throwable first. Other exceptions still propagate.

cards.front: What does MethodHandles.tryFinally wrap?
cards.back: A target handle plus a cleanup handle, like a try-finally block
cards.extra: The cleanup takes a Throwable, then the target's result, then the original arguments. It always runs, whether or not the target succeeded.

cards.front: Which method reorders a handle's arguments?
cards.extra: It also takes the target handle and the new MethodType. The index array names, in order, where each new argument comes from.

cards.front: Which method binds fixed values to leading arguments?
cards.extra: Callers then supply only the remaining arguments. Supplying a bound one again fails with WrongMethodTypeException.

cards.front: In foldArguments, where does the combiner's result go?
cards.back: Into the argument immediately before the folded ones
cards.extra: That reserved slot is why the folded arguments must come last. If the combiner returns void, the target needs no extra slot.

cards.front: In which JDK were method handles introduced?
cards.extra: They were built to help compiler and language-runtime developers. They were never intended to replace reflection wholesale.

cards.front: What can reflection do that method handles cannot?
cards.back: List class members and inspect their properties
cards.extra: There is no enumeration in the Method Handle API. Method handles instead offer powerful wrapping and adaptation of invocation.

cards.front: How do you turn a reflective Method into a method handle?
cards.extra: It requires the lookup class to have permission for that member. unreflectGetter/unreflectSetter do the same for a Field.

cards.front: When is reflection appropriate to use?
cards.back: When a program must examine or modify runtime behaviour
cards.extra: It is an advanced feature that needs solid language fundamentals. Extensibility, tools and debuggers are its classic uses.

cards.front: Which three drawbacks does reflection carry?
cards.extra: Each comes from dynamic resolution and from reaching members the compiler would forbid. Prefer non-reflective code where possible.

cards.front: Why are reflective operations slower than direct calls?
cards.back: Types are resolved dynamically, blocking JIT optimisations
cards.extra: Including inlining and devirtualisation. Avoid reflection in hot, performance-sensitive paths.

cards.front: How can a module restrict reflection?
cards.back: By not opening its package to another module
cards.extra: A named module can prohibit access to its own internals at runtime. That is why deep reflection into the JDK's internals largely stopped working.

cards.front: What is the danger of accessing private members reflectively?
cards.back: It breaks abstractions and can surprise on an upgrade
cards.extra: Accessing private fields produces illegal-in-normal-code behaviour, which may create portability and correctness problems.

cards.front: Why do debuggers and test harnesses rely on reflection?
cards.back: To inspect private members and call discovered APIs systematically
cards.extra: A debugger needs to see what the language hides. A test harness can enumerate methods and call them to raise coverage.

cards.front: Which Reflection classes implement AnnotatedElement?
cards.extra: Any of them exposes annotation discovery. Class also models enums, records and even arrays.

cards.front: Which method tests whether a specific annotation is present?
cards.extra: The argument must be an annotation class, or the code will not compile. It returns a boolean.

cards.front: Which two methods return an array of annotations on an element?
cards.extra: The array is empty if none are present. The declared variant includes annotations on that element only, excluding inherited ones.

cards.front: How do getAnnotations() and getDeclaredAnnotations() differ?
cards.extra: The plural forms return arrays. The singular variants, getAnnotation and getDeclaredAnnotation, take a Class and return one instance.

cards.front: How do you read a repeating annotation that the compiler stored once?
cards.back: Read the container annotation, then call its value()
cards.extra: The class file holds a single @Validators, which encloses the repeated @Validators. Tedious but the only direct route.

cards.front: Which method returns repeated annotations without unwrapping the container?
cards.extra: It opens the container for you and returns an array. Use it whenever the annotation may repeat.

cards.front: Which annotation meta-annotation makes an annotation inheritable by subtypes?
cards.extra: Inheritance applies only through class extending, not through interfaces. Enums and records cannot be extended, so they gain nothing from it.

cards.front: Why is annotation inheritance meaningless for enums and records?
cards.back: They are final and cannot be subclassed
cards.extra: There is no subtype that could inherit. Annotation inheritance needs an actual extends relationship.

cards.front: Which interface models annotations on types in use, rather than declarations?
cards.extra: It covers annotations where a type appears, e.g. the type argument or the implemented interface. Declaration annotations are plain AnnotatedElement.

cards.front: Why must getConstructor() be wrapped in a try/catch?
cards.extra: The compiler demands handling because a missing constructor may exist at runtime. Reflection's lookups are not compile-time checked.

cards.front: Which methods are available on a Java array?
cards.extra: Arrays are implemented in the VM and have no dedicated class. clone() and length behave specially.

cards.front: How do you obtain an array's length reflectively?
cards.extra: The length itself is not part of the array's type, which is why it cannot be read from the Class object.

cards.front: Which method checks whether a Class represents an array?
cards.extra: It returns true for any array type, including multidimensional arrays. The component type is available separately.

cards.front: Which method gives an array class's element type?
cards.extra: For an int[] it returns int.class. For a nested array it returns the next array type.

cards.front: How do you create an array dynamically when its type is only known at runtime?
cards.extra: Any type and dimension is supported. It is the reflective equivalent of new T[n].

cards.front: Which methods read and write an array element reflectively?
cards.extra: Older code often uses these for primitive arrays; newer code uses per-primitive variants. Arguments must fit the component type.

cards.front: How can you avoid boxing when accessing a primitive array reflectively?
cards.extra: They skip conversion to Integer, Double and so on. That matters in tight loops over large primitive arrays.

cards.front: What happens if you pass a Float object to Array.setFloat for a float array?
cards.extra: The typed setters insist on the primitive or a value that widens losslessly. This is boxing leaking through the reflective API.

cards.front: Why is Array.setLong(arr, ...) legal on a long array but illegal on an int array?
cards.back: Widening int to long loses no precision; narrowing long to int does
cards.extra: So int values may be stored into long arrays, but not the reverse. The same rule applies to the primary reflection API.

cards.front: Which exception signals an index beyond the array's length?
cards.extra: It fires for both reads and writes. It is one of the few reflectively reached errors that are not wrapped.

cards.front: Why do most java.lang.reflect classes have no public constructors?
cards.back: They must be obtained through methods on Class
cards.extra: ReflectPermission is the deprecated exception. Direct construction would bypass the runtime's bookkeeping.

cards.front: How do you get the Class object from an instance?
cards.extra: This works for any reference type, since all inherit it from Object. Primitives cannot be dereferenced this way.

cards.front: Which suffix gives the Class object for a type without any instance?
cards.extra: It is the simplest way to get a primitive's Class. It also works for interfaces and arrays.

cards.front: What does Class.forName(name) throw for an unknown class?
cards.extra: The name must be fully qualified. It cannot be used for primitive types, but it does work for array classes.

cards.front: How does a name like [B arise?
cards.back: It is Class.getName()'s encoding of an array of bytes
cards.extra: One bracket per nesting level; the letter encodes the component type. [B is byte[].

cards.front: How does Class.getName() encode an array of long?
cards.extra: The letters are Z boolean, B byte, S short, I int, J long, C char, F float, D double. Note long is J, not L.

cards.front: How does Class.getName() encode an array of reference type N?
cards.extra: So String[] is [Ljava.lang.String;, and the canonical name is the readable java.lang.String[].

cards.front: How many characters does a three-dimensional int array's name start with?
cards.extra: One bracket per nested array, then the component code. This string can be passed back to Class.forName.

cards.front: Which method was added in Java SE 22 for primitive types by name?
cards.extra: It also accepts void. A non-primitive name yields null; a null argument throws NullPointerException.

cards.front: Which field of a wrapper class holds the Class of the primitive it wraps?
cards.extra: So Double.TYPE is identical to double.class. Void.TYPE is void.class.

cards.front: What does Class.getSuperclass() return for a class, and for Object?
cards.extra: It never returns interfaces: those come from getInterfaces(). The null is the top of the hierarchy.

cards.front: Does getInterfaces() return inherited interfaces?
cards.back: No - only those directly implemented or extended
cards.extra: To gather all interfaces, walk the superclass chain yourself. Arrays get Cloneable and Serializable.

cards.front: Which interfaces does every array class implement?
cards.extra: Arrays are Objects, so their type extends Object and carries those two. That is why arrays can be cloned and serialized.

cards.front: How do getClasses() and getDeclaredClasses() differ?
cards.back: getClasses gives public member classes including inherited ones
cards.extra: getDeclaredClasses returns all member classes of this class only, private ones included. The latter exposes helpers such as Character$CharacterCache.

cards.front: What does getDeclaringClass() return for an anonymous class?
cards.extra: An anonymous class has no name and thus no declaring class. Its enclosing class can still be found with getEnclosingClass().

cards.front: How do declaring class and enclosing class differ?
cards.back: Enclosing is the class it is written inside; declaring only exists for members
cards.extra: For a member class they are the same. For an anonymous class, getDeclaringClass is null but getEnclosingClass is not.

cards.front: Which interface do Field, Method and Constructor share?
cards.extra: It provides getDeclaringClass for each member, plus modifiers and related queries. That is why the three look alike in the API.

cards.front: Which method returns all declared constructors, private ones included?
cards.extra: The array reflects public, protected, package-private and private. The non-declared forms return public ones only.

cards.front: Which method returns only the public constructors as an array?
cards.extra: Use the declared variants when you need the full list. A private constructor is invisible here.

cards.front: Can constructors be inherited, and does lookup include inherited ones?
cards.back: No, so there is no superclass lookup
cards.extra: That is why there is no analogue to getField reaching up the hierarchy. Each class's constructors are its own.

cards.front: Which method finds one constructor by parameter types?
cards.extra: The declared variant also sees private constructors. Types must match exactly, so byte[].class denotes a byte array parameter.

cards.front: How do you obtain a constructor's raw parameter types?
cards.extra: The generic variant getGenericParameterTypes() returns a Type array. There you call getTypeName().

cards.front: Which method returns the exceptions a constructor declares?
cards.extra: The generic variant returns Type objects instead of Class objects. Both expose what may be thrown.

cards.front: Why is Class.newInstance() deprecated?
cards.back: It only calls the no-arg constructor and bypasses exception checking
cards.extra: It also requires the constructor to be visible. Constructor.newInstance() has none of those limitations.

cards.front: Which exception wraps an exception thrown by the constructor itself?
cards.extra: Use getTargetException() to reach the real cause. It is part of reflective invocation for methods too.

cards.front: What does InstantiationException mean from newInstance?
cards.back: The class cannot be instantiated, e.g. an interface or abstract class
cards.extra: A private or non-existent constructor is instead an access problem. IllegalAccessException covers that case.

cards.front: What does setAccessible(true) do on a constructor?
cards.back: Suppresses the access-control checks, letting it be called
cards.extra: It does not change the constructor's modifiers. Module restrictions may still block it.

cards.front: How is a record's canonical constructor available reflectively?
cards.back: It is generated by the compiler and found as any other constructor
cards.extra: You did not write it, so lookup uses the component types. An empty record can also be built via its no-arg constructor.

cards.front: Why does getConstructor() throw NoSuchMethodException?
cards.back: No matching no-arg or typed constructor exists
cards.extra: The check happens at runtime rather than compile time, so the code must handle it explicitly. This is normal for reflective lookups.

cards.front: What is dependency injection in one sentence?
cards.back: You delegate object creation to a factory that initialises collaborators
cards.extra: The factory checks fields and supplies their values, so the business object never builds its own dependencies. Ordering of initialisation is centralised.

cards.front: How is a bean factory implemented in Java without injection infrastructure?
cards.back: A class with getInstanceOf(Class, args...) using reflection
cards.extra: It derives the argument types, finds the matching constructor and invokes it. The caller passes the class to build.

cards.front: To find a constructor reflectively, why must argument types match exactly?
cards.back: getConstructor matches declared types, not widened ones
cards.extra: Passing a String where the constructor takes CharSequence throws NoSuchMethodException despite the assignability.

cards.front: How do you extract the runtime types from the args passed to a factory call?
cards.back: A stream of arg.getClass() over the arguments
cards.extra: That array of Classes is then handed to the constructor lookup. Null arguments break this approach, as their type is unknown.

cards.front: How is the singleton pattern implemented most simply in this factory?
cards.back: A registry keyed by the bean class
cards.extra: On a hit it returns the existing instance. On a miss it creates one, stores it, and returns that.

cards.front: Which collection type provides a thread-safe instance registry?
cards.extra: Its putIfAbsent is atomic, which avoids external synchronisation. Null values are not permitted in most implementations.

cards.front: Why does putIfAbsent alone not guarantee a single instance?
cards.back: Several threads may each create an instance; only one is stored
cards.extra: The losers still hold their own newly built object. So after the put you must read the value back, as get, to return the winner.

cards.front: What is the atomic sequence for a singleton registry?
cards.extra: The get-after-put closes the race. Synchronising the entire path would also work, but causes contention.

cards.front: How does the factory perform field injection?
cards.back: Scan declared fields, select those annotated, and set an instance
cards.extra: The correct type is instantiated through the same factory, so singletons are honoured. setAccessible(true) is called even on public fields.

cards.front: Why call setAccessible(true) before setting an injected field?
cards.back: The field is typically private, so otherwise access is refused
cards.extra: It suppresses the access check. Calling it on a public field is harmless but redundant.

cards.front: Is there a java.lang.reflect.Enum class?
cards.back: No - and none is needed, since enums are classes
cards.extra: Enum constants are public static final fields, so most reflective operations work unchanged. Only a few APIs are enum-specific.

cards.front: Which three reflection APIs are enum-specific?
cards.extra: The first tests the type, the second lists the constants, the third tests a field. Everything else uses the ordinary class API.

cards.front: How do you list an enum's constants when you have no instance?
cards.extra: It returns the constants in declaration order. Without an instance it is the only route, since the enum cannot be instantiated.

cards.front: What is the relation between getEnumConstants() and values()?
cards.back: They return equal arrays, in the same declaration order
cards.extra: values() is added by the compiler; getEnumConstants is the reflective equivalent. Both give the constants as declared.

cards.front: What parameters does an enum's generated constructor take, beyond any you declare?
cards.extra: These are appended to your own declared parameters. The constructor is private, which is why the constants are the only instances.

cards.front: Can reflection add new constants to an enum at runtime?
cards.extra: The private constructor can be located, but invoking it to add a constant fails. This immutability is part of enums' safety.

cards.front: Which field does the compiler generate holding all constants?
cards.extra: It backs the public values(). It also appears in the reflective field list.

cards.front: Which compiler-generated methods appear on every enum?
cards.extra: The first two are public API; the third is an internal helper. Lambda-generated methods also show up if the enum uses lambdas.

cards.front: How do you read the value of an enum's static field reflectively?
cards.extra: A static field belongs to no object. Passing an instance is pointless and may mislead readers.

cards.front: Which field modifier marks an enum constant?
cards.extra: Each constant is a public static final field whose name is the constant's identifier. That is why Field.isEnumConstant() can test it.

cards.front: Which field-lookup method returns public fields including inherited ones?
cards.extra: Only public fields are returned. The declared forms stay local and reach private members.

cards.front: Which method returns private fields, but not inherited ones?
cards.extra: They return everything declared in this class whatever the modifier. Superclass fields are absent.

cards.front: Which method gives a field's type as a Class?
cards.extra: It works when the type is not generic. For a generic field, the result is the erased type, usually Object.

cards.front: For a generic field of type T, what does getType() return?
cards.extra: Type variables disappear at compile time. You need the generic query to recover the declared type.

cards.front: Which method returns a field's generic type?
cards.extra: It returns a Type, whose getTypeName() gives the readable name. It reflects only the declared signature, not runtime type arguments.

cards.front: Can getGenericType() tell you the real runtime type argument?
cards.back: No - only what was written in the source
cards.extra: A Box<String> field still reports Box<T> from the declaration. Java's erasure leaves no runtime record of the argument.

cards.front: What does Field.getModifiers() return, and how do you decode it?
cards.back: An int bitmask, decoded with static Modifier methods
cards.extra: Bit 0 set means public, bit 3 means static, and so on. Each Modifier method tests one flag.

cards.front: Which method, added in Java SE 20, reads modifiers as a set?
cards.extra: It is far more readable than bit tests. Note that modifiers and access flags are not one-to-one.

cards.front: Why do field accessors require the target object as an argument?
cards.back: The Field object is shared by all instances
cards.extra: One Field represents the field declaration, not a value. Which instance you mean must be supplied at each call.

cards.front: Why do all instances of a class share one Field object per field?
cards.back: There is exactly one Class object per class
cards.extra: The Class object and its members model the declaration, not the values. That is why both Field.get and Field.set demand the target instance.

cards.front: Does setAccessible(true) change a field's access modifier?
cards.back: No - it only suppresses the access check
cards.extra: The field is still declared private and remains so for normal code. This common misconception surprises many developers.

cards.front: Which superclass holds the setAccessible method for fields, methods and constructors?
cards.extra: All three extend it, so the whole family shares the flag. The class also holds related accessibility queries.

cards.front: What may still block setAccessible(true)?
cards.back: A named module that has not opened the package
cards.extra: By default a module is closed to reflection, including from the unnamed module. Opening requires a declaration or an explicit flag.

cards.front: What happens to final fields after setAccessible(true)?
cards.back: They can be written, despite the final modifier
cards.extra: Reading works regardless. Since JDK 26 a warning is issued when a final field is mutated reflectively.

cards.front: Which fields remain un-writable even after setAccessible(true)?
cards.extra: These are explicit exceptions. Records make their instance fields unmodifiable to preserve their immutability guarantee.

cards.front: Which methods avoid boxing when reading or writing primitive fields?
cards.extra: They exist for every primitive type. Use them in hot loops where boxing would allocate.

cards.front: What happens if you call Field.setInt on a field of type Integer?
cards.back: An IllegalArgumentException - the types do not match
cards.extra: The typed accessors require the exact primitive. A wrapper field needs the general Object forms.
